results.message: How did someone become a Christian in your church?

voice_event.speaker: lpc
voice_event.text:
You are taught before you are washed. We tell you what you are joining before you join it. You say the creed back, and then we baptize you. That is the center of it. What comes before the water is not a brief ceremony. Augustine wrote a whole guide to how the teaching should be done. After the water, the bishop preaches to you, week after week, already baptized and sitting with the rest of the congregation. That is how what we hold actually reaches an ordinary believer. Not by handing you a written doctrine to memorize. By the voice of the man answerable for you, telling you to your face what he thinks you need.

And the road into the church was not only for those who had never been inside. Someone who had failed could come back, and the way back was a road too. There was an order to it, the order took time, and everyone could see it. Discipline was the road; reconciliation was the arrival. Augustine says to correct with words, or blows if need be, yet forgive in the heart, as a surgeon cuts from kindness: “Let us rebuke with words, and with blows if need be. But let us also forgive the sin and cast the fault out of our hearts. The Lord added ‘from your hearts’ for this reason: when discipline is given out of love, gentleness must not leave the heart. For what is as kind and gentle as a surgeon with his knife?”

glosses.plain_meaning: Discipline is the road; reconciliation is the arrival. What matters is that it is a road at all. There is an order to it, the order takes time, and everyone can see it.
glosses.quick_meaning: For us, reconciliation is not a quiet, private pardon. It is a public road that a failed member walks, in stages, back into the community.
glosses.translational_sense: A modern listener may hear either a brief private confession behind a screen, or a therapeutic notion of reconciliation -- repair achieved once both parties feel differently. Neither is private and neither is primarily about feeling for us. This is a public, staged, community-witnessed process with an examined entry, a real duration, and a formal act of readmission at the end, controlled by one office. What it restores is standing, and the whole community can see it being restored.
false_friend: a private sacramental confession, a few minutes long, said alone with no public witness
a therapeutic reconciliation between two parties, complete once both simply feel differently toward each other

names.name: Augustinius of Hippo Regius, presbyter 391, bishop 395/396-430

figures_used.bridge_line: Our bishop at Hippo. The people seized him and brought him to be made a presbyter while he wept. Later they pressed him into the bishop's office over his own refusal. He spent his last days weeping over psalms of penitence, while an army lay outside the walls.

dates.display: converted 386, baptised 387; seized by the congregation at Hippo and ordained presbyter against his own wishes in 391, weeping through it (Possidius, Vita IV); designated coadjutor and consecrated bishop of Hippo by Megalius, primate of Numidia, in 395/396, again amid popular acclamation (Possidius, Vita VIII); died 430, during the Vandal siege of Hippo

confidence.divergence_note: Epistles XX-XXI are our own rare exception to the episcopal-voice monopoly -- two lay confessors, neither yet ordained, writing to each other in the first person (Author-Gravity-Risk: Yes). Even there the transaction itself is clerical and confessor-side; the reconciled believer does not speak anywhere in our record.

The text field is the NPNF English as printed. modern_rendering follows the Latin of PL 38 where the English departs from it: 'cast away the remembrance of it from the heart' renders culpam de corde abjiciamus, cast the fault out of the heart, and the Latin does not ask for forgetting; 'though through affection' renders si per charitatem, when discipline is given out of love.
